title: Answer to Question: On the Darfur Crisis
text:
Answer to Question on the Darfur Crisis

Question: The Darfur crisis in Sudan has escalated in a striking manner. So what is the reality of this crisis, and who is behind it? And why has the government of Sudan left it to worsen?

Answer: The Darfur issue was raised in a (hot) manner during the ongoing negotiations between the movement of the rebel Garang and the Sudanese government. Three factors have contributed to its emergence and worsening:

Local competition over land and pastures; external interference and stirring of the problem; and, before this and after it, the government of Sudan's neglect of looking after the affairs of its citizens with the care that Islam obliges, with justice and goodness.

As for the local competition: in Darfur reside the African (Fur) tribes and other tribes of Arab origins. The conflict in Darfur began with the decrease in natural resources against a great increase in livestock and in cultivated area, and the desire of some of the Arab tribes of camel herders to own land because of their need for grazing. In return, the African (Fur) tribes refused to share the land and pasture with the Arabs, considering themselves its owners as an inheritance from the forefathers.

The rebellion began relying on the Zaghawa tribe, and they wanted to bring in other tribes, and began terrorising them by raiding and imposing levies. So the tribes found themselves before two choices: either join the rebellion or set up militias to protect them from the raids. So these tribes set up militias, which quickly became strong with the spread of weapons in Darfur, as they come to it from the neighbouring states. This led to the worsening of the situation and its increasing badness and complexity day after day. Thousands of lives have been taken, hundreds of villages have been burned, and hundreds of thousands have been displaced from their homes, having no bed or cover except the earth and the sky, and some of them fled to Chad in the hope of escaping the hell of Darfur.

As for the external interference and stirring of the problem: those who stirred up the events of Darfur and brought about the crisis are the Europeans, and specifically France and Britain. The evidence for that is that the rebels from the African Fur tribes were given support from Chad, whose rulers are agents of France, in terms of supplies and in terms of a base of operations and refuge, and London worked as a media platform for the leaders of the rebel movement.

As for America, it tried to cover for its agent al-Bashir by confining itself to statements, and it did not order al-Bashir's government to stop suppressing the rebels, though it was able to do that. But after the crisis worsened and turned into a humanitarian catastrophe, the humanitarian organisations and the United Nations, pushed by Europe, pressured Sudan and demanded that it stop supporting the Arab militias (the Janjaweed), which carried out acts of abuse against the Africans, as is rumoured.

After the media shone the light on the events of Darfur in terms of the numbers of dead, who reached thousands, and of the displaced, who reached a million refugees, and after these media described what is happening in Darfur as the greatest humanitarian catastrophe of this age, and that the international community must intervene immediately because its non-intervention means the death of thousands of Africans monthly, after all of that America found itself compelled to intervene, to ride the wave and to lead it. It ordered the Sudanese government to stop the tragedy by way of several demands, among them sending 6000 Sudanese police to Darfur to preserve the security of the African citizens, and dissolving the Janjaweed militia and disarming them. Sudan's representative at the United Nations stated that the mentioned police force had been completed on 22/7. When he was asked about the period needed to disarm the Janjaweed, he said no one knows.

But the Europeans were not content with these American measures, and demanded imposing sanctions on Sudan and sending foreign, non-Sudanese forces to Darfur. And Europe, especially France, began to cast doubt on America's role in imposing sanctions on Sudan.

Meanwhile, the British position was strangely hostile against the Sudanese government, and Britain was behind embarrassing America through incitement, exaggeration and issuing provocative statements against the Sudanese government.

America wanted the Darfur problem not to be raised until after finishing the subject of the South and the signing of the agreement between Garang and the Sudanese government, and proceeding in the steps of that to accomplish them, and then moving on to Darfur. As for Europe, France and Britain, it wanted to raise the problem and heat up the situation at the same time, to create troubles for al-Bashir's government, which is loyal to America, in order to topple it or penetrate it.

The chargé d'affaires of the American embassy in Khartoum, Gerald Gallucci, stated in mid-May 2004 CE that the situation in the Darfur region in the west of the country represents a vital subject in the file of human rights in Sudan, and he added that he has reservations about linking the peace process in the South to achieving peace in the Darfur region. This indicates that America is seeking to complete the arrangements for separating the South and then move on to concentrating on the subject of the regions of the North.

But Europe, France and Britain, realised this point, so it concentrated on raising the Darfur problem militarily, politically and in the media to embarrass America and destabilise the situation of al-Bashir's rule, which is loyal to America. After America had been able to have the effective role in the subject of the South and had marginalised Europe's role in it, Europe, France and Britain, wanted to have an influential role in Darfur that would compensate for its weak role in the South.

Nevertheless, America appears as if it wants to block the road to Europe in the Darfur problem; therefore it took the reins of initiative and presented on 22/7/2004 CE a draft to the Security Council (currently being discussed) warning Sudan to put matters right and giving it a deadline of a month, otherwise it would be exposed to sanctions, whereas Europe wanted military intervention and sanctions without a deadline. Powell stated, during his meeting with Annan, to the press on 22/7: there is no need for the military solution now; rather, the Sudanese government must treat this problem. That is, he did not agree with Blair's statement on the same day, 22/7/2004, not ruling out military intervention in Sudan. And he proposed sending (5000) of his forces to Darfur.

This does not mean that America wants good for Darfur; rather, it wants evil, but gradually, until it finishes completely with completing the separation of the South which it began. Europe realises the danger of this plan of America's, so it moved the subject now to destabilise the current rule of Sudan, which is loyal to America, and at the same time so that Europe holds part of the threads of the Darfur issue and is not marginalised as happened in South Sudan, where America took charge of the subject.

In conclusion, America was compelled to take these measures against the Sudanese government after it was embarrassed before international public opinion because of the Darfur crisis, which was exaggerated in a rapid and sudden manner. Had the problem remained within reasonable limits internationally, and under control, and not been magnified, America would not have intervened; but the one who exaggerated it is other than it, and specifically France and Britain.

Thus external interference and stirring have a principal role in the Darfur rebellion.

As for the government of Sudan's neglect of looking after the affairs, and its blundering in treating the matter, it is clear from leaving this problem to grow and worsen, even though the like of these problems in tribal regions is a usual matter. Darfur is a Sudanese region located in the west of Sudan on the border with Chad, and the area of this region is approximately equal to the area of France. It is inhabited by Arab and African tribes, all of them Muslims. The region was named Darfur after the African "Fur" tribes, and the Arab tribes such as the Zaghawa came and shared with them in living, in religion and in destiny.

The problems that usually occurred between the tribes were traditional and simple, relating to the areas of farming, irrigation and grazing and the water points, and these problems would quickly find a solution through the tribal leaders. It is known that this type of problem is considered something normal in all tribal regions, and they are of the type of natural disputes that arise in mobile tribal societies.

But these disputes, instead of the state resolving them with wisdom, awareness and good looking after of affairs, by working to provide pastures for the owners of livestock and to provide the requirements of farming and irrigation for the owners of the lands, the village dwellers, and that by gathering the two parties and looking after them without discrimination and preventing the problem from being made a field for interference, the state did the opposite of that. It left matters between the Muslims, Arabs and Africans, to worsen and become complicated, with the African militias spreading in it supported by France by way of Chad, fed in the media by way of Britain, then from behind a curtain by way of the rebel of the South, Garang, and then the Arab militias supported by the state. Thus everything became mixed up, crime spread and people were displaced, and the state left the militias fighting each other without itself, as a state, putting a limit to that by looking after the affairs of the two parties. Had America not been embarrassed by Europe and so intervened and ordered the government of Sudan to intervene as a state in solving the problem, the militias would have remained fighting each other in a field empty of the state and its order.

Thus, instead of al-Bashir's government absorbing those militias and concluding reconciliation between the tribes, it escalated and used its army's ground and air forces in supporting the Janjaweed, and thereby ignited the spark of bloody conflict between the Muslims. Then it began to blunder in solving the problem and to wait for the solution from other states; indeed, to wait for it from John Garang, the rebel of the South who separated the South from Sudan. Its Foreign Minister stated on 14/5/2004, saying (You, addressing Garang, have a relationship with the rebel forces in Darfur, and you must have a positive role in solving the issue). And before that the government official responsible for the Sudanese governmental committees in charge of implementing the government's recommendations in Darfur stated (The final solution of the problem in Darfur must be by way of John Garang, after the problem of the South is solved and he comes to Khartoum to serve as Vice-President, because Garang is the most capable of solving such disputes, as he has long experience in them).

These officials say this while they realise that Garang's movement feeds the rebellion in Darfur. The Foreign Minister of Sudan, in one of his press interviews dated 14/05/2004 CE, answered the question of a journalist: Do you consider Garang's movement responsible for the rebellion in Darfur? The minister answered: Yes. Nevertheless, the officials of Sudan ask Garang to solve the problem for them, and there is no doubt that the solution he wants for the Darfur region is that it secede from Sudan as the South seceded.

Thus the abasement of the government of Sudan has reached the point of asking the leader of the rebellion of the South to treat the rebellion of Darfur!

The Sudanese government is still dealing with the situation in a manner that will inevitably lead to the worsening of the situation in Darfur and other regions of the North. Despite its knowledge that the relief organisations transport weapons to the rebels there, it agreed to the resumption of those organisations' work there, and agreed to the African monitoring teams, which will provide cover for the rebels so that they are able to gather their ranks and prepare for rebellion anew. When the Sudanese Foreign Minister was asked in the same interview mentioned above: Are you happy with this agreement that allows Ugandan forces to enter southern Sudan? He answered: "Are you happy with everything you do? Sometimes you do things because necessity requires them." And this is due to his knowledge of what the like of those forces will do in stirring up rebellion and supporting it.

What is astonishing is that the government condemned the withdrawal of the so-called humanitarian United Nations organisations from Darfur, asking them to stay to look after the affairs of the citizens of Darfur, while the government knows before others that these organisations only work to spread fitnah, smuggle weapons in relief boxes and contact the hotbeds of rebellion, as happened with the United Nations aeroplane that was caught transporting weapons and equipment to the rebels in Darfur, and before it the Red Cross aeroplane. Instead of condemning the withdrawal of those organisations, it was obligatory on the government to take charge itself of looking after the affairs of its citizens with justice and goodness.

The laxity, cowardly abandonment and submissiveness of the government towards those fateful issues is the first and fundamental cause of such calamities. Instead of intervening in Darfur in a manner that pulls the rug from under the feet of the agents calling for rebellion, by explaining the Shar'i rule on dividing wealth in a region inhabited 100% by Muslims, we find it cowering before the international institutions, IGAD, the American enemy and the European Union, especially France, Germany and Britain, which announced openly in broad daylight its readiness to send military forces to Darfur, as came in Blair's previous statement. Thus the country has become a field for international interventions. Nevertheless, the government asks for solutions to the Darfur problem from Garang, and from America behind him, thinking that as long as the rule in Sudan is compliant to America, it will support it and preserve it in all circumstances, whereas America gives no weight to its agents if their existence conflicts with its interests, or if they have exhausted the roles entrusted to them.

Then, by its concessions in the South in response to the orders of the master of the White House, we find it opening the door to rebellion in all parts of Sudan on various pretexts, political or economic. Everyone knows the extent of the grinding economic crisis from which Sudan suffers despite the richness and multiplicity of its natural resources, and that is due only to the government's failed policies, because of its contravention of the Shar' of Allah, and because it does not refer for judgement to what Allah has revealed, and does not look after the affairs of the subjects with justice and goodness.

This is what the Sudanese Interior Minister Abdel Rahim Hussein confirmed, commenting on the events of Darfur: «It seems that the demands of the rebels in Darfur have become like what the negotiators in the South demand, such as the right of self-determination and having an independent army».

Ceding any span of the land of the Muslims to be under the authority of the Kafir enemy is a major crime in Islam, and it encourages other regions to secede, and it likewise creates in the enemy the boldness to demand more concession. For any concession, even if small, opens the door wide for more concession.

Whoever is made lowly, lowliness becomes easy upon him; a wound gives no pain to a dead man.

And what took place of concession in Palestine and Indonesia, and what is taking place in Sudan, speaks of that.

It is strange, and likewise painful, that the (opposition) parties in Sudan, which almost oppose the government in everything, nevertheless agree with the government in the crime of ceding the South to the authority of the rebel Garang, by America's planning and arrangement, and likewise in what is taking place of negotiations with the rebels in Darfur, which may end in what the South ended in. This exposes the bad reality that the parties which call themselves opposition are in, and that they do not fear Allah in squandering the lands of the Muslims.

The solution before Sudan does not go beyond one of two, the first:

That it persists in falsehood and continues the policy of concession, relying on America in treating its issues, and making the country a field of struggle between America and Europe.

And the second: that it returns to the truth, and returning to the truth is a virtue, and follows the Shar' of Allah, so it cancels its agreement with Garang, stops its talks with the rebels of Darfur, and treats the issue of the unity of the country on the basis that it is a vital issue which it is not permitted to squander under any circumstance; for it is an issue of life or death.

As for the first, concession and cowardly abandonment, it drags the country into a major calamity: of humiliation and weakness, division, disintegration and ruin, and betrayal of Allah, His Messenger and the believers.

And as for the second, it is might and invulnerability, unity of the body and union and prosperity, and the pleasure of Allah, glorified be He, and of His Messenger (saw).

So will the rulers in Sudan desist, and choose what pleases Allah and His Messenger, and make honourable stands that will benefit them in this world and the Hereafter?

11 Jumada al-Akhirah 1425 AH

28/07/2004 CE
